Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Value Name: Very Expensive (>10% of household income for basic service)
revision_notes: The originally cited source (energycapitalpower.com) was fetched and found to be a general renewable-transition article that does not itself state a tariff figure, so it did not directly support the $0.23/kWh claim in the comments. Fresher and more authoritative sources were fetched and read: the US government's Country Commercial Guide (2022) records an average tariff of $0.23/kWh, 'one of the highest in the world'; the Gambia's 2025 Draft National Energy Compact (NAWEC/Government of the Gambia, with World Bank/Mission 300 partners) states an average domestic tariff of $0.21/kWh; and a June 2026 news report on the World Bank's Gambia Public Finance Review 2026 confirms tariffs still average $0.21/kWh and are 'among the highest globally', driven by weak utility financial performance and system losses. Against a 2024 GNI per capita of $880 (World Bank Atlas method, roughly $73/month), a basic monthly consumption band costs well over 10% of per-capita income for lower-income households. Score of 1 (Very Expensive) confirmed and updated to the most current (2026) authoritative source.
revised_comments: Electricity in the Gambia is very expensive relative to household income. The World Bank's 2026 Gambia Public Finance Review and the Government's 2025 National Energy Compact both put the average domestic tariff at around $0.21 per kWh, which the World Bank describes as among the highest in the world in US dollar terms. Against a GNI per capita of around $880 (2024), the cost of a basic monthly electricity consumption band represents well above 10% of income for lower-income households. High tariffs stem from NAWEC's dependence on imported heavy fuel oil, currency depreciation and weak utility financial performance, which the World Bank flags as a persistent barrier to affordability and to expanding access.

Definition: Percentage of total electricity generation from renewable sources (hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, biomass). Indicates energy sustainability and potential for distributed power solutions relevant to ICT infrastructure in off-grid areas.
Comments: Low renewable share ~2% per IRENA, small solar capacity
revision_notes: The originally cited source (energycapitalpower.com) was fetched and confirmed on-topic: it cites IRENA data showing only 2MW of installed solar PV at end-2022 and a national target to raise the renewable share from 2% to 40% of the mix by 2025 (a target not met), directly supporting the original ~2% estimate. This was cross-checked against two further primary-type sources: an IRENA-sourced generation-statistics aggregator (countryeconomy.com) puts renewable generation at 1.06% of total output in 2024 (5 of 512 GWh) and 0.98% in 2023, and the World Bank/IEA WDI indicator (EG.ELC.RNEW.ZS) records 1.6% for 2021, the latest year published. All of these measure domestic generation and sit firmly in the <10% band, consistent with the metadata's cited primary sources (IRENA, WDI). However, the Gambia's 2025 Draft National Energy Compact (NAWEC/Government of the Gambia) states a materially different figure: renewable energy's share 'in the generation mix, including imports' is currently 13%, against a 2030 target of 30%, reflecting imported OMVG regional hydropower rather than domestic generation. Because this is a genuine definitional ambiguity (generation vs. total supply mix including imports) that would move the score from 1 to 2 under an alternative reading, and because the two readings diverge materially, this row is flagged for human review rather than resolved by assertion. Score of 1 recalculated on the generation-only definition used by the variable's primary sources, but the 13%-inclusive-of-imports figure should be checked against the intended scope of the indicator.
revised_comments: Renewable sources contribute a very small share of the Gambia's domestically generated electricity, estimated at around 1% of total output in 2024 (IRENA/World Bank data), reflecting a heavy reliance on imported heavy fuel oil for thermal generation and only a small-scale (single-digit MW) domestic solar base. This falls well short of the government's earlier National Development Plan target of raising the renewable share from 2% to 40% by 2025. Donor-backed projects, including a 23 MW solar plant at Jambur financed by the World Bank and European Investment Bank, are intended to expand renewable capacity. Separately, the Gambia's 2025 National Energy Compact reports a renewable share of around 13% for the overall power supply mix once imported regional hydropower is included, against a 2030 target of 30%, illustrating that the picture differs materially depending on whether imports are counted.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
revision_notes: Both originally cited World Bank SDG7 Tracking pages were fetched and confirmed live and on-topic. The most recent published figures (2023) show urban electricity access of 85.3% against rural access of 35.3%, a gap of 50.0 percentage points, slightly wider than the 47.5pp stated in the original comments (which used a marginally lower urban figure of 82.8%). This remains comfortably within the 41-60pp band. Score of 2 confirmed unchanged on the same primary sources, with the comments figure corrected to match the source data precisely.
revised_comments: World Bank SDG7 Tracking data (ESMAP/World Bank) show that 85.3% of the Gambia's urban population had access to electricity in 2023, compared with 35.3% of the rural population, a gap of 50.0 percentage points. This substantial urban-rural disparity persists despite overall national electrification progress, which separate reporting places at around 74% by 2024, up from 56% in 2017, reflecting that grid connections and off-grid solutions have so far concentrated disproportionately in and around the Greater Banjul Area relative to more remote rural regions.
